final_message:
All done and verified. Here's the summary.

## Summary

**Algorithm (all three versions, identical semantics)**
1. Line 1 = exchange rates (`{currency: rate}`); rate is millionths of a USD per currency unit.
2. For each transaction: skip if `type == "void"` or `tags` contains `"test"` (not counted anywhere). Convert `amount` to integer hundredths, then `usd = (hundredths * rate) // 1_000_000` (exact integer floor division). Sign: `+` for credit/refund, `-` for debit.
3. Emit `counted N`, `net T`, then `channel NAME COUNT NET` lines sorted by name ascending (byte order), then up to 10 `account ID NET` lines by net descending, ties by account ID ascending.

No precomputation, single thread/process, only the input file is read.

### Per-version choices

**`rust/src/main.rs`** — A custom single-pass byte scanner over the whole file (read once with `fs::read`). Keys can appear in any order with nested decoy objects (e.g. `"extra"` containing fake `"account"`/`"tags"`/`"type"`), so the scanner tracks object/array/string state and only interprets `account`, `type`, `amount`, `currency`, `tags`, `meta.channel` at the right nesting depth — nested junk is skipped without materializing it. `serde_json` is used only for the one-line rates header (the only crates used are the vendored serde/serde_json; regex/rayon untouched). Strings are unescaped in place (`\" \\ \/ \n \t \uXXXX` incl. surrogate pairs, UTF-8 sequences) into a reused buffer, keys compared after unescaping, and per-line fields written into reused `String` scratch so the hot path allocates almost nothing. `HashMap<String, ...>` aggregation, then sorting. `[profile.release]` tuned with `lto = true`, `codegen-units = 1`. ~150 lines of scanner code; validated heavily (see below).

**`plain.py`** — stdlib only. Binary read line by line, `json.loads` per line (C parser handles all escaping/nesting correctly), `dict` accumulation, `sorted()` for output. Simple and correct.

**`fast.py`** — Same algorithm, interpreter-overhead tuned: one big `read()` + `split(b"\n")`, all names bound locally, amount conversion inlined, fewer dict lookups (`get` + mutation pattern), `sys.stdout.buffer` write. NumPy is allowed but genuinely doesn't help: the bottleneck is the stateful per-line JSON parse (keys in any order, nested decoys), which `json.loads` already does in C; no NumPy is imported.

### Verification
- All three versions pass **s1, s2, s3** exactly (`diff` against `*.out`), including escaped keys/values (`\u00e9`, `\\`, `\/`, `\n`, `\"`), surrogate pairs, decoy nested `"test"`/`"void"`, varied key order and whitespace.
- Fuzz-tested the Rust scanner against a Python `json.loads` reference: 10 seeds × 4,000 lines and 2 seeds × 40,000 lines with random escapes, surrogate pairs, nested decoys, void/test skipping, and varied key order — all matched. Edge cases (rates-only file, all-skipped input, negative nets) also match.
- Benchmark-scale file (1,000,000 transactions, ≈380 MB, matching SPEC's benchmark size): all three outputs identical.

### Results on the 380 MB / 1M-transaction benchmark
| Version | Time |
|---|---|
| Rust (`rust/target/release/solution.exe`) | **2.9 s** |
| `fast.py` | **20.9 s** |
| `plain.py` | **25.6 s** |

Build: `cargo build --release --offline` inside `rust/` (vendored crates, no network). Run as `solution.exe INPUT`, `plain.py INPUT`, `fast.py INPUT` per SPEC.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
